title: How to Ask for a Recommendation Letter: Emails and Preparation

content:
Choose a referee who knows your work well enough to give specific examples. Ask early, explain the application and provide a short information pack that helps them write an accurate recommendation.

The templates, adapted per relationship

The two templates in this guide serve different referees and should not be confused. The professor template leads with the shared work: 'you supervised my dissertation on X, graded at Y' — the referee's memory is jogged by specifics they can verify from their own records. The professional template leads with observable outcomes: the project delivered, the responsibility held, the timeframe. Both close the same way: deadline, method, and a clear statement that a short letter is fine. Referees write more for applicants who reduce their uncertainty than for applicants who flatter them.

Two habits protect the relationship. Send each referee the submitted application outcome afterward — a two-line thank you with where you got in, because referees remember and re-use letters for prizes, next degrees and jobs. And never ask a referee to submit at midnight before a deadline; if the timeline has collapsed, say so plainly, give them the minimum viable packet, and accept that the letter may be shorter than you hoped.

Who should write your recommendation?

Choose someone who has directly assessed your academic work, research, employment or professional contributions and can give specific examples. A senior title is less important than an informed, credible recommendation. Confirm whether the programme requires academic rather than professional referees.

The request timeline referees actually need

Reference letters fail on logistics more than on willingness, and the failure starts with the ask. Four weeks is the honest minimum: week one for the request and materials, week two for writing around teaching, week three for the reminder that rescues most letters, week four as buffer before the deadline. Each week has a job, and skipping one transfers work to your referee — the person you most need to keep happy. Brief every referee with the same packet: the deadline date and exact submission method, the programme's stated criteria, your CV, the project or work you are claiming, and two sentences on which of your work they should attest.

Choose attestors over titles. A seminar leader who watched your thesis take shape writes stronger evidence than a famous professor who taught you in a 300-person lecture. And stack choices against risk: one supervisor, one subject specialist, one professional or teaching referee covers the angles UK panels read for — research ability, subject depth and collegiality. The charts quantify the schedule and the packet.

[[chart:rec-weeks]][[chart:ref-packet]]Ask early and make it easy to write an accurate letter
  1. Read how many referees are required and how submission works.
  2. Ask the potential referee if they can write a supportive, specific recommendation.
  3. State the programme or award and the exact deadline.
  4. Supply your CV, transcript, project details and the selection criteria.
  5. Send a respectful reminder before the deadline if needed, and thank them afterward.

Email template: asking a professor

Subject: Recommendation request for [programme] — deadline [date]

Dear Dr [Surname],

I took [course / research project] with you in [term/year], where I worked on [specific assignment or project]. I am applying to [exact programme] at [institution], and I wanted to ask whether you would feel comfortable writing a strong academic recommendation for me.

The submission deadline is [date, time and time zone], and the university sends referees a secure upload link. If you are able to help, I can send my CV, transcript, statement and a short summary of the work I completed with you.

Thank you for considering my request.

Best regards,
[Name]

Email template: asking an employer

Subject: Reference request for [degree/scholarship] — [date]

Dear [Name],

I am applying for [programme/award], which requests a professional reference. Since we worked together on [specific responsibility], I wondered if you would be comfortable commenting on [relevant skills supported by your observations].

The deadline is [date], and I can share the criteria and submission instructions. Please feel free to decline if you do not have sufficient time.

Kind regards,
[Name]

Polite reminder template

Subject: Gentle reminder — recommendation due [date]

Dear [Name],

Thank you again for agreeing to write my recommendation. The deadline for [programme] is [date and time zone]. I wanted to check whether you received the submission link and whether I can provide anything else useful.

Many thanks,
[Name]

What information should you provide?

ItemWhy it helps
CV and transcriptProvides dates, courses and achievements to verify
Programme and criteriaShows what the selection panel needs
Relevant project summaryRefreshes the referee’s memory of specific work
Submission link/instructionsAvoids portal errors
Deadline with time zonePrevents last-minute confusion

Avoid these mistakes

  • Writing a fictional letter for a referee to sign unless they specifically request an accurate draft and the rules permit it.
  • Requesting a reference on the deadline day.
  • Sending an undocumented list of exaggerated achievements.
  • Submitting a letter yourself when the programme requires direct referee submission.
  • Assuming every scholarship accepts professional references.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use the same referee for several applications?

Often yes, with their permission. Give a clear list of deadlines and programme requirements.

What if a referee declines?

Thank them and ask someone with direct knowledge of your work. It is better to receive a specific letter from an appropriate referee than a generic one from a famous person.

Give your referee a manageable information pack

Send the programme name, deadline and submission instructions, together with your CV and a short reminder of work the referee supervised. Explain why you are applying and which relevant tasks they observed. If several applications are involved, put the dates in one clear table. Ask whether they can provide a supportive reference before listing their details. A suitable reminder might say: “The reference portal closes on [date]. Please let me know if you need any further material from me.” Do not write achievements on their behalf or ask them to confirm work they have not seen.

Choose the referee by what they observed

Before asking, write down what each potential referee could describe accurately. A dissertation supervisor might discuss research decisions and independence. A lecturer might know a substantial assignment, while an employer might describe responsibility and teamwork. Use the programme's rules to establish which types of referee are accepted; do not assume a professional reference can replace a required academic one.

The request should give the person a comfortable way to decline. Ask whether they can provide a supportive reference for the particular application, rather than listing their details first and hoping they agree. If they cannot help, thank them and approach another suitable person. Their title matters less than their ability to discuss relevant work with examples.

Keep a reference tracker

ItemWhat to recordWhy it helps
ProgrammeExact course and institutionPrevents a request intended for one application being confused with another.
DeadlineDate, time and time zoneGives the referee the actual submission target.
SubmissionPortal invitation or other official methodHelps identify a missing link without sharing confidential letters.
MaterialsCV, criteria and relevant work summaryProvides factual reminders while leaving the judgement to the referee.
StatusAgreed, invited, submitted or unresolvedMakes one useful reminder possible without repeated chasing.

If several applications are involved, send one clear list of dates rather than a series of disconnected messages. Tell the referee when a portal invitation is generated and ask them to check spam if it does not arrive. Follow the university's troubleshooting instructions if the system fails.

Keep the referee's judgement independent

Provide accurate information, not a script of praise. If a referee asks for a draft and the application rules permit one, keep every claim factual and allow them to revise or reject it. Never submit a confidential reference yourself when the university requires direct submission from the referee.

Can I ask someone who taught me several years ago?

Yes, if they can still assess relevant work and the programme accepts that reference. Reintroduce yourself with the course, dates and specific assignment or project. Offer a brief factual summary rather than assuming they remember every detail.

Questions applicants often ask

How far in advance should I ask for a recommendation letter?

Four weeks minimum: one week for the request, two for writing with a mid-point reminder, one as buffer. Academic referees juggle dozens of commitments; the ask gives them a realistic window, the reminder at week two saves most letters.

Who should write my PhD reference letters?

One supervisor-type referee, one subject specialist who saw your research thinking, and one professional or teaching referee. Choose people who can attest specific work over impressive titles — specifics beat seniority in panel reading.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date.
